Elemental Boron and
Metal Borides

The cluster bonding met in the boranes reappears in the solid state: the element is built from B12 icosahedra, and the borides from B atoms, chains, nets and polyhedra.

P. A. Mohammed Ziyad · Department of Chemistry, Farook College (Autonomous), Kozhikode

The last deck of the series. It goes back to the element itself and to its compounds with metals. The main message is continuity: the three-centre bonds and the Wade counts used for molecules also explain these solids.

Orientation slide.
Learning outcomes

By the end of this deck you should be able to

  • Explain why boron, alone in group 13, is a hard, high-melting non-metal built from clusters.
  • Describe the B12 icosahedron and count its 36 electrons in α-rhombohedral boron.
  • Outline the structures of α-R12 and β-R105 boron and of boron carbide.
  • Relate the M : B ratio of a metal boride to the way its boron atoms are linked.
  • Use electron counting to explain MgB2, CaB6 and the boron-rich borides.
  • Outline how metal borides are prepared, and relate their properties to their uses.
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2–13.3.
Read the outcomes. Outcomes 2 and 5 are where earlier decks (3c–2e bonds, Wade's rules) are used again.
Part A

The element

Three valence electrons, four orbitals, and nowhere to hide.

A
Part A places boron in its group and explains why its structure must be unusual.
The element

Boron is the odd one out in group 13

propertyBAlGaInTl
m.p. / K2453933303430577
b.p. / K42732792247723551730
ΔHat / kJ mol−1582330277243182
I1+I2+I3 / kJ mol−168885140552150835438
χ (Pauling)2.051.611.761.661.79
rcov / pm88130122150155
  • The ionisation energies are too high for B3+ to exist: boron chemistry is covalent.
  • The atom is small and has 3 electrons for 4 orbitals (2s, 2px,y,z).
  • A metal would need many delocalised electrons; a simple covalent net would need four. Boron does neither: it forms multicentre bonds in clusters.
  • The result is a black, very hard (≈ 9.3 Mohs), semiconducting solid with one of the highest melting points of any element.
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), Table 13.1.1 (m.p. for β-rhombohedral boron); hardness and semiconducting behaviour: Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), §6.2 (recalled values).
Point to the m.p., b.p. and atomisation enthalpy: boron's are far above Al's even though Al is the metal. The bonding in solid boron is strong and three-dimensional. Note that published melting points vary (about 2350–2450 K) because pure boron is hard to obtain and molten boron attacks containers (Deck 1).
How the picture developed

Two centuries from isolation to structure

Why so slow?

Pure boron was hard to make (Deck 1), and many "allotropes" reported before 1960 turned out to be boron-rich borides or carbides. Only two forms, α-R12 and β-R105, have been fully solved by X-ray diffraction.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2, §13.3.1; Decker & Kasper, Acta Cryst. 1959, 12, 503; Hoard et al., J. Solid State Chem. 1970, 1, 268; Nagamatsu et al., Nature 2001, 410, 63; Oganov et al., Nature 2009, 457, 863; Zhai et al., Nature Chem. 2014, 6, 727; Mannix et al., Science 2015, 350, 1513 (citations after 1970 and the 1959/1970 details are recalled).
Use the timeline to connect with Deck 1, where the isolation of boron was discussed. The structures of the element came only with X-ray crystallography, and new forms are still being found.
Part B

The B12 icosahedron

The common unit of the element, boron carbide, many borides and B12H122−.

B
Part B looks at one icosahedron and at how its electrons are used.
The B12 icosahedron

12 vertices, 30 edges, 20 triangular faces

B12 unit from α-boron (Ih ideal)
drag to rotate
  • Mean B–B edge 177 pm; cage diameter ≈ 334 pm.
  • 36 valence electrons. Each edge is not a 2c–2e bond: there are far too few electrons for 30 bonds.
  • Same cage as B12H122− (Deck 7): in the solid, the exo B–H bonds are replaced by bonds to other icosahedra.
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2, Fig. 13.2.2; Wade (1971), Fig. 3-22 (edge 177 pm, diameter 334 pm); Muetterties (1967), ch. 1, p. 8.
Rotate the model to find the 5-fold, 3-fold and 2-fold axes shown in the figure. In α-boron the icosahedron is very slightly distorted, so the model edge lengths range from 1.75 to 1.81 Å.
The B12 icosahedron

Inside one cage: 3 two-centre and 10 three-centre bonds

  • For a closo-Bn skeleton Li gives 3 2c–2e bonds and (n − 2) BBB 3c–2e bonds.
  • For n = 12: 3 + 10 = 13 bonding pairs = 26 electrons.
  • This is Wade's n + 1 = 13 skeletal pairs (Deck 6), and Lipscomb's styx picture of B12H122− (Deck 4).
  • MO view (Wade): the 12 radial and 24 tangential orbitals give 36 cage MOs, of which 13 are bonding.

Bond valence

One 3c–2e bond makes up a shortfall of four electrons and counts as a bond valence of 2 shared over three atoms.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2, Figs. 13.2.3–13.2.4; Wade (1971), §3 (13 bonding MOs of 36); see Decks 4 and 6.
This is the same count students did for closo-boranes. The canonical form drawn is one of many resonance forms; the MO picture avoids choosing one.
The B12 icosahedron in the solid

Where do the 36 electrons go in α-boron?

  • Each icosahedron forms six 2c–2e bonds to icosahedra in the layers above and below (one electron from each B), and takes part in six 3c–2e bonds within its layer (⅔ electron from each B): 26 + 6 + 4 = 36.
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2, p. 463 (26 + 4 + 6 = 36); B12H122− count from Deck 6.
Build the bars one at a time. The comparison with B12H12 2− is the key point: both have a 26-electron cage, but the anion has two extra electrons from the charge. The solid compensates by using three-centre links between icosahedra in the same layer.

Allotropes of boron

Simple formula, complicated structures.

C

Allotropes

Many reported, two fully solved

R/T = rhombohedral/tetragonal; the number is the atoms in the primitive cell. All forms contain B12 icosahedra. α-R12 has α = 58.06°, close to the 60° of a regular ccp lattice.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2, p. 461–463; * γ-B28: A. R. Oganov et al., Nature 2009, 457, 863 (recalled; not in the course texts).
Stress Li's warning: many reported allotropes are really boron-rich compounds, stabilised by a few per cent of C, N or metal.
Allotropes

α-R12 boron: close-packed icosahedra

one layer ⊥ c: six neighbours, six 3c–2e links (violet)
drag to rotate
  • Each icosahedron has 12 neighbours: six in its layer and three in each layer above and below, as in ccp.
  • In the layer: three equatorial B atoms from three icosahedra meet in a B–B–B 3c–2e bond (B···B ≈ 202 pm). In Li's drawing each node is such a bond, not an atom.
  • Between layers: polar atoms form normal 2c–2e bonds (≈ 167 pm, shorter than the cage edges).
  • Open space between icosahedra: α-boron has a low density (≈ 2.46 g cm−3).
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2, Fig. 13.2.1; distances computed from the α-boron coordinates (a = 491.8, c = 1258.1 pm, hexagonal setting; B. Will, B. Kiefer, Z. Anorg. Allg. Chem. 2001, 627, 2100, recalled); density: Greenwood & Earnshaw (recalled).
Use the buttons. In the layer view, the small violet spheres mark the centres of the 3c–2e bonds. In the stacked view, teal bonds are the 2c–2e links between layers. Ask: why is the inter-layer bond shorter than a cage edge? Because it is a full electron-pair bond between two atoms, whereas cage edges share electrons among several atoms.
Allotropes

β-R105 boron: the B84 unit, shell by shell

1. central B12 icosahedron
drag to rotate
  • 105 atoms in the rhombohedral cell (a = 1014.5 pm, α = 65.28°).
  • Shell 1: a central icosahedron (B–B ≈ 168 pm from the centre).
  • Shell 2: 12 atoms, one bonded outward from each vertex (≈ 330–340 pm from the centre).
  • Shell 3: 60 atoms (≈ 435–460 pm), the bases of twelve pentagonal pyramids; together they form a C60-like B60 cage.
  • B84 units are joined through B10–B–B10 groups: 84 + 21 = 105.
Model from G. A. Slack, C. I. Hejna, M. F. Garbauskas, J. S. Kasper, J. Solid State Chem. 1988, 76, 52 (COD 9017507; sites with occupancy ≥ 0.5; shell radii computed); Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2, Fig. 13.2.5.
Build the unit in three clicks. Each of the 12 violet atoms is the apex of a pentagonal pyramid whose base lies in the teal B60 shell; the pyramid is half an icosahedron. Partially occupied sites in the CIF are left out.
Did you know?

New forms of boron are still being found

  • γ-B28 (2009) forms above about 9 GPa. Its B12 icosahedra and B2 pairs carry small opposite charges, like a salt made of one element.
  • B40 (2014), the first all-boron cage, was called "borospherene" by analogy with C60.
  • Borophene (2015) is a one-atom-thick boron sheet grown on silver. Unlike graphene it has holes in its triangular net: three electrons cannot fill a full triangular lattice.

3 electrons per atom
↓
triangles, clusters,
holes in the net

Oganov et al., Nature 2009, 457, 863; H.-J. Zhai et al., Nature Chem. 2014, 6, 727; A. J. Mannix et al., Science 2015, 350, 1513 (all recalled citations; pressure value approximate).
These facts come from general knowledge rather than the course texts; check them before setting exam questions. The common thread is electron deficiency: boron cannot form a simple graphite-like or diamond-like structure.
Part D

Metal borides

More boron, more B–B bonding.

D
Part D classifies metal borides by how their boron atoms are linked.
Metal borides

As boron content rises, boron links up

Metal-rich (M4B to M2B)

Isolated B atoms in metal cages; behave like interstitial compounds.

Intermediate (M3B2 to MB2)

Pairs, chains, double chains, then planar nets.

Boron-rich (MB4 and beyond)

3D networks of octahedra, cubo-octahedra or icosahedra; metals sit in cages.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.1, Fig. 13.3.1; uses: high m.p., hardness, wear resistance, rocket cones and turbine blades (Li, p. 464).
Several hundred binary borides are known. Borides are hard, high-melting and chemically resistant, which is why they are used in rocket cones and turbine blades.

Metal borides · MB2

MgB2: graphite-like boron sheets

MgB2: B nets (orange), Mg (green)
drag to rotate
  • Hexagonal, P6/mmm; a = 308.6, c = 352.4 pm, Z = 1.
  • B–B = 178.2 pm (= a/√3). Each B sits in a Mg6 trigonal prism.
  • Mg atoms are sandwiched between B6 hexagons.
  • AlB2 has the same structure (B–B 175 pm) and gives its name to the type.
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.1(1), Fig. 13.3.2; isoelectronic B−/C analogy and incomplete transfer: general textbook treatment (e.g. Greenwood & Earnshaw).
The B⁻ ≡ C analogy is the simplest way into MgB2. It is only approximate: the real charge transfer is less than complete, and the holes left in the boron σ bands are important for superconductivity.
Did you know?

A shelf chemical that superconducts

  • MgB2 had been known and sold for decades before Akimitsu's group found in 2001 that it becomes superconducting at Tc = 39 K.
  • That is about twice the Tc of Nb3Sn, the material used in the magnets of NMR spectrometers, and its properties are similar.
  • It is a "conventional" superconductor: light boron atoms vibrate fast, and the B–B σ bonds couple strongly to these vibrations.

39 K

MgB2, 2001

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.1(1) (Tc 39 K, 2001; comparison with Nb3Sn); J. Nagamatsu, N. Nakagawa, T. Muranaka, Y. Zenitani, J. Akimitsu, Nature 2001, 410, 63 (recalled citation); mechanism: recalled, simplified.
Nb3Sn has Tc about 18 K. MgB2 superconducting wires can be cooled with cryocoolers or liquid hydrogen rather than liquid helium, which is one reason for continuing interest.
Metal borides · MB6

CaB6: B6 octahedra linked in three dimensions

Ca in a cage of eight B6 octahedra (CsCl-like)
drag to rotate
  • Cubic: B6 octahedra at the cube corners, joined along all six axes by B–B bonds; Ca in the 24-coordinate cage (CsCl-like packing of Ca and B6).
  • Calculations show a net transfer of only 0.9–1.0 e, not 2: this is why metal-deficient M1−xB6 and even KB6 are stable.
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.1(3), Fig. 13.3.3; Wade (1971), §3 (6 + 14 electrons per B6); first MO treatment: Longuet-Higgins & Roberts, Proc. R. Soc. A 1954, 224, 336; model built from a = 414.5 pm, B at (x, ½, ½), x ≈ 0.20 (recalled parameters).
The count is Wade's rule again: a closo-B6 needs 7 skeletal pairs (14 electrons), and the six exo bonds now go to neighbouring octahedra instead of H atoms, as in B6H6 2−. Formally the framework is [B6]2−. LaB4 in panel (a) has chains of B6 octahedra joined by B2 pairs.
Metal borides · MB6 and MB4

Other hexaborides, and the tetraboride LaB4

  • M2+ (Ca, Sr, Ba, Eu): fill the framework's bonding levels; semiconductors or poor metals.
  • M3+ (La and early lanthanides): one electron more than the framework needs. It enters a conduction band, so LaB6 is a metal.
  • Fewer electrons: because the real transfer is ≈ 1 e, M1−xB6 and KB6 survive.
  • Small late lanthanides (Ho, Er, Tm, Lu) are too small to fill the 24-coordinate MB6 site; they form MB4 instead, with M–B 185–200 pm.
LaB4 (Kato et al. 1974), 2 cells along c
drag to rotate

LaB4 (ThB4 type, tetragonal)

Chains of B6 octahedra run along c, linked sideways in the ab plane by B2 pairs into a 3D framework. The La atoms sit in tunnels along c.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.1(2), (3), (5), Fig. 13.3.3(a); model from K. Kato, S. Kawai, C. Oshima, I. Kawada, Acta Cryst. B 1974, 30, 2933 (COD 2105437) (M–B range for MB4, p. 466); LaB6 metallic behaviour: general literature (recalled).
The electron count is a guide, not an exact rule, for solids. The framework tolerates a range of electron counts, and the extra electrons decide the electrical properties. LaB4 combines two motifs seen earlier: B6 octahedra (as in CaB6) and B2 pairs (as in M3B2).
Metal borides · rare earths

For rare-earth borides, ionic radius decides the structure

Large ions (La–Gd, Eu2+) form MB6; small ones (Tb–Lu, Y) form YB12, AlB2 and YB66 types; MB4 forms across the whole series.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), Table 13.3.2 (redrawn as a chart).
Read the chart row by row. The cut-off for MB6 is between Gd and Tb: smaller ions rattle in the 24-coordinate cage. YB12 needs the smaller ions too.
Metal borides · boron-rich

Boron-rich borides: B12 cubo-octahedra and giant clusters

  • Two kinds of B12: a cubo-octahedron (square and triangular faces) in YB12, and an icosahedron in NaB15.
  • They are related by small displacements: the square faces fold into pairs of triangles (compare the diamond–square–diamond process, Deck 7).
  • YB66: Fm3̄c, a = 2344 pm, Z = 24. Unit: a B156 cluster, B12⊂(B12)12: one icosahedron surrounded by twelve.
  • B–B within icosahedra 171.9–185.5 pm; between icosahedra 162.4–182.3 pm. 336 more B atoms per cell are statistically disordered.
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.1(4)–(5), Fig. 13.3.4, p. 466–467.
YB66 has about 1600 atoms in the unit cell. It shows the icosahedral hierarchy again: twelve icosahedra round a central one, like the B84 unit in β-boron.

Metal borides · boron-rich

Cubo-octahedron ⇌ icosahedron

twelve B atoms, 24 fixed edges (grey) + 6 square diagonals (violet)
drag to rotate
YB12NaB15

  • A cubo-octahedron has 8 triangular and 6 square faces; an icosahedron has 20 triangles.
  • Twist the 8 triangles in turn and pull them inward: each square folds along one diagonal into two triangles.
  • When the 6 diagonals (violet) become as short as the edges, the cage is an icosahedron: 24 + 6 = 30 edges.
  • In borides the shift is small: Li's arrows show the displacements that relate YB12 to NaB15.
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.1(4), Fig. 13.3.4; animation: vertices (0, ±a, ±b) and cyclic permutations with constant edge length, a/b from 1 (cubo-octahedron) to 1/φ (icosahedron), computed for this deck.
Press play or drag the slider. The same continuous motion (sometimes called the "jitterbug") connects the two B12 polyhedra. Compare the diamond–square–diamond process in carborane isomerisation (Deck 7).

From isolated atoms to frameworks

What to notice

B–B bonds are 160–185 pm throughout, close to those in the boranes. Only their number per atom changes: 0 (isolated), 1 (pairs), 2 (chains), 3 (nets) and 4–5 (polyhedra).

Preparation

Six routes to metal borides

methodexampleconditions, notes
1. Direct combination of the elementsTi + 2 B → TiB2
Mg + 2 B → MgB2		arc-melting, sintering or hot-pressing; most general route
2. Reduction of the metal oxide by boronSc2O3 + 7 B → 2 ScB2 + 3 BO↑high temperature, vacuum; volatile boron suboxide removed
3. Reduction by carbon and B4C (or B2O3)Eu2O3 + 3 B4C → 2 EuB6 + 3 CO
TiO2 + B2O3 + 5 C → TiB2 + 5 CO		carbothermal; the usual industrial route
4. Co-reduction of mixed oxides by Al, Mg or NaTiO2 + B2O3 + 5 Mg → TiB2 + 5 MgOstrongly exothermic; can run as self-propagating synthesis; MgO leached with acid
5. Co-reduction of volatile halides by H2TiCl4 + 2 BCl3 + 5 H2 → TiB2 + 10 HClchemical vapour deposition of thin, pure coatings
6. Electrolysis of fused saltsmetal oxide + B2O3 (or borax) in a fluoride meltboride crystals deposit at the cathode (e.g. hexaborides, TiB2)
Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), §6.3.1 (methods and the Sc2O3, Eu2O3 examples; recalled); other equations written for this deck and balanced; MgB2 from the elements: Nagamatsu et al. (2001).
All the routes need high temperatures, because the products are refractory. The choice depends on the product: bulk powders by methods 1, 3 and 4; coatings by CVD (method 5); single crystals by fused-salt electrolysis or from metal fluxes. Ask students to check that each equation balances.
Properties

Properties follow from the boron framework

  • Refractory: TiB2, ZrB2 and HfB2 melt above ≈ 3000 °C, higher than the parent metals.
  • Hard and stiff: strong B–B and M–B bonding; B4C and TiB2 are among the hardest materials known.
  • Electrical: metal-rich and transition-metal MB2 borides are metallic; TiB2 conducts better than titanium itself. Boron-rich borides such as B4C are semiconductors.
  • Chemically resistant: most transition-metal borides resist non-oxidising acids; they are attacked by hot oxidising acids and alkaline oxidising melts.
  • Oxidation: in air at high temperature a B2O3 glaze forms and protects the surface until it evaporates (above ≈ 1100 °C).
  • Hydrolysis: borides of electropositive metals react with acid. Stock's boranes came from "magnesium boride" + HCl (Deck 1).

Trend with boron content

More boron gives more B–B bonding, lower density, greater hardness and more covalent, less metallic behaviour.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3 (high m.p., hardness, wear resistance, chemical resistance); Wade (1971), §4-3 (hydrolysis of magnesium boride); m.p., conductivity and oxidation values: Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), §6.3.2 (recalled, approximate).
Link each property to the structure: the framework of B–B bonds makes borides hard and refractory, and electrons not needed by the framework make many of them metallic. The hydrolysis point links back to Stock's work in Deck 1.
Uses

Borides at work

materialproperty usedapplication

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), p. 464 (refractory uses, rocket cones, turbine blades), §13.3.1(1) (MgB2); Muetterties (1967), ch. 1 (metallurgical promise, limited by cost); other applications: Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), §6.3 and general literature (recalled).
Muetterties noted in 1967 that borides showed promise in metallurgy but were too expensive. Several of these uses (TiB2 cathodes, ZrB2 ceramics, MgB2 wire) have since become practical.
Did you know?

The strongest magnets are borides

  • Nd2Fe14B magnets were reported in 1984, independently by Sagawa (Sumitomo) and by Croat (General Motors).
  • They are the strongest permanent magnets in common use: in hard-disk drives, earphones, electric-vehicle motors and wind turbines.
  • Only about 1 % of the mass is boron. It is a metal-rich boride: each B atom is isolated in a trigonal prism of Fe atoms, the first class in the catenation table.
Nd2Fe14B unit cell (Herbst et al. 1984)
drag to rotate
M. Sagawa et al., J. Appl. Phys. 1984, 55, 2083; structure: J. F. Herbst et al., Phys. Rev. B 1984, 29, 4176 (COD 1540077); J. J. Croat et al., J. Appl. Phys. 1984, 55, 2078 (recalled citations; structural detail from general literature).
General knowledge, not from the course texts; verify before examining. A good example of a metal-rich boride with isolated boron atoms.
Part F

Boron carbide and its relatives

α-boron with a three-atom chain added.

F
Part E looks at boron carbide, the most important non-metal boride.
Non-metal borides

Boron carbide: B11C icosahedra and C–B–C chains

  • Homogeneity range B1−xCx, 0.1 ≤ x ≤ 0.2, including B13C2 and B4C; space group R3̄m.
  • Derived from α-R12 boron by adding a linear C–B–C chain along [111].
  • B4C (a = 520 pm, α = 66°) is B11C(CBC), not B12(CCC): one C sits in each icosahedron, statistically.
  • B12P2 and B12As2 are analogues with a P–P or As–As link instead of the three-atom chain.

Uses

One of the hardest materials after diamond and c-BN: abrasives, armour plate. Rich in boron, so ¹⁰B makes it a neutron absorber in reactor control rods.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.2(1), Fig. 13.3.5; uses: Greenwood & Earnshaw (1997), §6.3 (recalled).
Make the connection with α-boron explicit: same icosahedral net, with the open space along the threefold axis filled by a three-atom chain. Muetterties (1967) already grouped elemental boron, boron carbide and borides as solids to be described by multicentre bonds.
Non-metal borides

B2O3 and borosilicate glass

  • B2O3 is the main oxide. Fused, it dissolves many metal oxides to give coloured borate glasses.
  • Its main use is in glass: borosilicate glass (Pyrex) has a small coefficient of thermal expansion and good workability.
  • Here boron is not electron-deficient in the borane sense: trigonal BO3 and tetrahedral BO4 units, with O→B π donation as in BX3 (Deck 2).

Boron's main markets

About half of boron production goes to glass and ceramics. Other uses: soaps and cleaners, fluxes for welding and soldering, fire retardants, plant nutrients and neutron shielding.

Muetterties (1967), on the U.S. market of the 1960s.

Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.3.2; Muetterties (1967), ch. 1 (uses); BO3/BO4: see Deck 2.
A short slide to round off the solid-state chemistry. The point to make is the contrast: B–O compounds are electron-precise because oxygen donates π density, as nitrogen does in borazine (Deck 9).
Summary

Key points

  • With 3 electrons for 4 orbitals, boron is a hard, high-melting non-metal built from B12 icosahedra (B–B 177 pm).
  • One icosahedron has 26 cage electrons (3 2c + 10 3c bonds); in α-R12 the other 10 go into six 2c and six 3c inter-icosahedral bonds.
  • β-R105 is built from B84 = B12@B12@B60 plus B10–B–B10; boron carbide is α-boron plus a C–B–C chain.
  • In metal borides, rising B content gives isolated B → pairs → chains → nets (MB2) → polyhedra (MB4, MB6, MB12, MB66).
  • MgB2 (B− ≡ C) superconducts at 39 K; CaB6 needs 20 e per B6 but only ≈ 1 e is transferred; ion size selects rare-earth boride structures.
  • Borides are made at high temperature from the elements, by reduction of oxides (B, C/B4C, Mg/Al), by CVD or by fused-salt electrolysis; they are refractory, hard and often metallic (TiB2, ZrB2, LaB6, MgB2, B4C).
Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2–13.3; Wade (1971), ch. 3.
Ask students to redo the CaB6 and α-boron counts on the board.
Check your understanding

Questions (press → to reveal each answer)

1. Why is boron not a metal like aluminium?
Its small size and high ionisation energies favour covalent bonds, but 3 electrons for 4 orbitals cannot give a simple 2c–2e net; it forms multicentre bonds in B12 clusters instead.
2. Account for the 36 valence electrons of one icosahedron in α-boron.
26 in the cage (3 2c + 10 3c), 6 in six 2c bonds to adjacent layers, 4 in six in-layer 3c bonds (⅔ e each).
5. Why is LaB6 used as an electron source?
Low work function (≈ 2.7 eV), metallic conduction, high m.p. and low volatility.
3. Predict the boron arrangement in FeB and in TiB2.
FeB (MB): zigzag chains. TiB2 (MB2): graphite-like hexagonal nets (AlB2 type).
4. Why does KB6 exist although B6 "needs" two electrons?
Calculations show only ≈ 1 e is actually transferred to each B6 even in CaB6; the framework does not need the full formal 2 e.
6. Give a route to a thin TiB2 coating.
CVD: TiCl4 + 2 BCl3 + 5 H2 → TiB2 + 10 HCl on a hot substrate.
Based on this deck; Li, Zhou, Mak (2008), §13.2–13.3.
Question 3 uses TiB2, which is not in the table; it is an AlB2-type boride, so students must apply the rule.
Looking back

One idea, from diborane to borides

1–2  B2H6: too few electrons for ethane-like bonds → the 3c–2e B–H–B bridge.
3–4  Higher boranes: 3c bonds in cages; Lipscomb's styx bookkeeping.
5–6  Reactions and Wade's rules: n + 1 skeletal pairs decide closo, nido, arachno.
7–8  Replace BH by CH or a metal fragment: carboranes and metallaboranes, same counts (isolobal).
9  Add a lone pair (N): borazine and BN, no longer electron-deficient.
10  Extend to solids: B12 in boron, B6 in CaB6, nets in MgB2, the same electron counting.
Muetterties (1967), ch. 1 (multicentre bonds in hydrides, elemental boron and borides); Wade (1971); Mingos, 50th anniversary review (2021).
Close the series by showing that one idea, electron deficiency handled by multicentre bonding, links molecules and solids.
